articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden defense mechanism in aging muscles that sacrifices strength to protect cells from damage. In mice, partially restoring a crucial molecule reversed signs of muscle wasting and prevented premature death, raising hopes for new treatments for age-related muscle decline.
articles.content:
Muscles naturally become weaker as we get older, but scientists have discovered that some of the changes associated with aging may actually help protect muscle cells from damage. New research reveals why aging muscles shift toward a different type of muscle fiber and identifies a crucial molecule that could offer a new approach to treating muscle loss.

Muscle tissue contains bundles of fibers with different functions. Fast-twitch fibers produce powerful, rapid movements but fatigue relatively quickly. Slow-twitch fibers, by contrast, support sustained activity and contain higher concentrations of mitochondria, the cellular structures responsible for producing much of the energy muscles need.

As people age, muscle strength declines and mitochondria become less efficient. Surprisingly, aging muscles also develop a greater proportion of slow-twitch fibers, even though these fibers depend heavily on the very mitochondria that are losing their ability to function. Researchers have observed similar changes in several conditions that cause muscle wasting.

This raises an important question: Why would muscles increasingly rely on an energy-producing system that is becoming less effective?

A Crucial Molecule Linked to Muscle Aging

To investigate this puzzle, scientists focused on cardiolipin, a specialized fat molecule located almost exclusively within the inner membrane of mitochondria. Cardiolipin helps maintain the membrane's distinctive folded architecture, which is essential for proper mitochondrial activity.

When cardiolipin is lacking, mitochondria struggle to generate sufficient energy. They also become less capable of producing the chemical signals and essential materials that cells require to function.

The researchers discovered that cardiolipin levels decrease in muscle mitochondria from both mice and humans as they age or experience disease. This decline was accompanied by structural abnormalities in the mitochondria and a loss of normal function.

To determine whether reduced cardiolipin directly contributes to these changes, rather than simply occurring alongside them, the team experimentally lowered cardiolipin levels in young mice.

The results closely resembled what happens during natural aging. Muscle fibers shifted away from the fast-twitch type toward slow-twitch fibers, matching the pattern previously observed in older mice and humans.

Even more strikingly, restoring cardiolipin to approximately two-thirds of its normal concentration began reversing muscle wasting and completely prevented the premature deaths seen in the affected animals.

Why Aging Muscles Sacrifice Strength for Protection

Further experiments revealed an unexpected explanation for the transformation. Rather than representing only a breakdown in muscle function, the shift toward slow-twitch fibers appears to be a protective response.

When cardiolipin concentrations fall, damaged mitochondria produce much larger quantities of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These highly reactive molecules can harm cellular structures, but they also play an important role in signaling that something is wrong.

The researchers found that ROS help initiate the transition from fast-twitch to slow-twitch muscle fibers. When they treated muscle cells lacking cardiolipin with an antioxidant to reduce ROS, the transformation became less pronounced.

A protein known as ERRγ plays a central role in coordinating this response. It directs cells to reorganize their mitochondria and change their muscle fiber characteristics. When scientists inhibited ERRγ in muscle cells grown in the laboratory, the transition between fiber types stopped entirely.

The team also discovered how the newly remodeled fibers help defend themselves.

Mice with insufficient cardiolipin absorbed considerably more glucose from their bloodstreams. However, their muscles were not primarily using this additional sugar to produce energy.

Instead, experiments that tracked specially labeled glucose showed that muscle cells redirected the sugar toward manufacturing their own antioxidants. This helped protect them against the damaging effects of excess ROS.

"The fiber switch is not the muscle failing, but the muscle trading power for protection. That's also why interfering with it can backfire: when we gave the mice antioxidants to mop up the ROS, their muscles fared worse, not better," says Assistant Professor Fabian Finger, first and co-corresponding author, from the University of Copenhagen.

A Potential New Approach to Treating Muscle Wasting

Although the findings point toward possible treatments for age-related muscle decline, the experiments demonstrating the protective mechanism and reversal of muscle wasting were conducted in mice. Human muscle samples were used only to establish that cardiolipin levels also decrease with age in people.

Nevertheless, researchers already have some ways to influence cardiolipin.

The FDA recently granted accelerated approval to elamipretide, a medication designed to help stabilize cardiolipin, for Barth syndrome, a rare inherited disorder. This suggests that targeting the molecule is medically feasible, although its effectiveness against ordinary age-related muscle loss remains unknown.

Another potential treatment target is ERRγ, the protein responsible for helping muscles adapt to mitochondrial stress.

ERRγ belongs to a family of proteins called nuclear receptors. These proteins are already established targets for approximately 10 to 15 percent of FDA-approved medications made from small molecules. Drugs that activate ERRγ are also being investigated in preclinical research for other medical applications.

The findings suggest that future therapies might work by restoring cardiolipin levels or by influencing the protective adaptations controlled by ERRγ.

"What encourages me most is that even a partial recovery of cardiolipin was enough to bring the muscle back. The question now is whether we can increase cardiolipin in aging muscle or target ERRγ to promote healthy adaptations. This is where the therapeutic potential lies," says senior author Zachary Gerhart-Hines, Associate Professor at the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research, University of Copenhagen.

The research involved scientists from more than 20 institutions. It was led by the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research at the University of Copenhagen in collaboration with the Center for Adipocyte Signaling at the University of Southern Denmark.

Financial support came from the Novo Nordisk Foundation, European Research Council, Lundbeck Foundation, US National Institutes of Health, and additional funding organizations.

The research is detailed, focused, and suggests concrete therapeutic potential, meeting all criteria for inspiring good news.
articles.personality_title: Scientists uncover molecule that protects aging muscles and reverses weakness in mice
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – As people get older, their muscles usually become weaker. Scientists have been trying to understand why this happens and if there is a way to stop or slow it down.

**What happened** – Researchers studied a special fat molecule called cardiolipin found inside mitochondria, the parts of muscle cells that produce energy. They found that as muscles age, cardiolipin levels drop. This causes muscles to change from fast, strong fibers to slower, more protective ones. In experiments with mice, partially restoring cardiolipin helped reverse muscle loss and prevented early deaths.

**Impact** – This discovery explains that muscles weaken partly because they protect themselves from damage by changing fiber types. It also shows that boosting cardiolipin could be a new way to treat muscle weakness caused by aging. This is important because muscle loss affects many older people and can reduce their ability to stay active.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to find ways to increase cardiolipin in human muscles or control a protein called ERRγ that helps muscles adapt to stress. Some medicines that affect these targets are already being tested for other diseases. Future research will check if these treatments can help older people keep their muscle strength.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Restoring a key molecule called cardiolipin may protect aging muscles and reverse weakness, opening new paths for treatments against muscle loss.

articles.title: Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. The finding reveals a hidden source of cardiovascular risk and could open the door to new treatments that protect the heart and brain.
articles.content:
Blood pressure readings are typically evaluated based on their average values, but growing evidence suggests that fluctuations throughout the day may be equally important. Rapid or excessive changes in blood pressure can independently increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and brain injury, even when average readings fall within the normal range.

Researchers at the University of Virginia School of Medicine have identified a small population of nerve cells in the brainstem that helps maintain steady blood pressure. The brainstem regulates essential involuntary functions, and these newly studied cells appear to limit blood pressure swings as people move between everyday activities, including sleeping, waking, standing, and exercising.

"What we found is that a loss of just a few hundred nerve cells leads to unstable blood pressure even though the mean blood pressure was normal," said UVA's Stephen Abbott, PhD, the lead investigator of the study. "This shows that the system that keeps blood pressure steady from moment to moment is no longer working."

A Hidden Brain Mechanism Behind Blood Pressure Problems

The same nerve cells have previously been found to be damaged or missing in people with multiple system atrophy, a rare, fatal neurological disorder related to Parkinson's disease. The condition is often accompanied by severe difficulties regulating blood pressure.

The new findings raise the possibility that disruptions involving these brain cells may also contribute to unstable blood pressure in other medical conditions, including cases where standard measurements show normal average levels. Understanding this mechanism could eventually help researchers develop treatments aimed at reducing harmful fluctuations and protecting against their potential consequences.

"Our work emphasizes a new appreciation for how we think about blood pressure problems," Abbott said. "It's not just about lowering the numbers - it's about keeping blood pressure stable from moment to moment."

New Research Could Change How Blood Pressure Is Treated

The findings were published in the scientific journal Circulation Research. The research team included George M.P.R. Souza, Harsha Thakkalapally, Faye E. Berry, Leah F. Wisniewski, Ulrich M. Atongazi, Daniel S. Stornetta, and Abbott. The researchers reported no financial interests related to the study.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health through grant HL148004.

The discovery also reflects the broader goals of UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute focuses on advancing research into difficult and complex diseases while helping promising laboratory findings move more quickly toward potentially lifesaving treatments for patients.

This breakthrough has broad implications for improving diagnosis and treatment of blood pressure-related health issues, potentially reducing risks of heart disease, stroke, and brain injury for a wide population. The article provides detailed context about the discovery, its significance, and future treatment possibilities, meeting the criteria for inspiring good news with meaningful real-world impact.

articles.title: How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03402-7Fresh ideas are welcome in a discipline in which progress is rare — provided they are applied rigorously.
articles.content:
Fresh ideas are welcome in a discipline in which progress is rare — provided they are applied rigorously.

Psychedelic-therapy clinics such as this one need to be accessible to all.Credit: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty

More than one billion people globally live with a mental-health condition. Collectively, these disorders are now the world’s leading cause of disability. Depression and anxiety alone cost the global economy an estimated US$1 trillion every year.

The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

Conventional pharmacological approaches to improving mental health are falling short. However, two Nature News features this week report on innovations that indicate a shift is under way. One describes the personalization of psychiatric care; the other discusses developments in psychedelic medicine. Although neither effort will provide a complete solution for the mental-health crisis, both are bringing much-needed ingenuity to the field.

To ensure that these ideas translate into improvements in mental-health care, they must be pursued with rigour and in a way that ensures they have the widest possible reach. As psychedelic-development programmes move towards regulatory approval, the US Food and Drug Administration has rightly clarified what types of evidence and outcome it expects to see in trials (see go.nature.com/4bstrh2). Funders and regulators must now ensure that approaches that prove successful actually reach the people who need them. This will not be straightforward because many psychedelics and proposed personalized treatments are expensive. They are developed with small groups of people with a specific condition in mind and therefore do not benefit from economies of scale. At the same time, personalized treatments can be out of reach for people from low-income backgrounds, who are more likely than others to have a mental-health condition.

Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks

Under the current psychiatric model for mental-health conditions, two people with the same diagnosis of depression can have distinct symptoms, different underlying biology and divergent responses to the same treatments. That heterogeneity is reflected in clinical outcomes. A substantial proportion of people don’t respond to the first antidepressant drug that they try, and around 30% remain symptomatic after trying several treatments (C. Njenga et al. BMJ 386, e073823; 2024).

In practice, conditions are more complex than conventional diagnostic categories suggest. One reason for this is that classifications have relied on subjective reporting of symptoms. Now, precision psychiatry approaches aim to improve diagnosis and outcomes. The idea is to personalize treatments by cataloguing symptoms in detail and as objectively as possible, and identifying measurable biological indicators, or biomarkers. The expectation is that this can help to match people with more-effective treatments, and do so faster by shortening the process.

Methods include the use of genetic and blood-based biomarkers; measures of brain activity such as functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalograms; and ‘digital phenotyping’, in which smartphones and other sensors record sleep and movement, for instance. But these assessments have yet to consistently yield improvements for people with mental-health conditions, as one of the features reports. Some researchers say that another approach would be to gather as much data as possible on how people respond to specific treatments and which responses correlate with mental-health improvements. Those data can then be fed into artificial-intelligence models to predict how individuals might fare. It is unclear, however, whether the benefits of such tools would outweigh their costs.

Psychedelics: concerns and opportunities

As reported in the other feature, psychedelics might tap into the brain’s capacity to reorganize its connections and circuits, potentially disrupting rigid patterns and enabling psychological changes — even for some people for whom conventional treatments haven’t worked.

The ‘bible for psychiatry’ is getting a rewrite: your guide to the next DSM

Outcomes could be optimized by personalization. But, as with precision psychiatry more broadly, this approach comes with a duty to prioritize research into treatment responses across diverse populations. The use of psychedelics introduces additional concerns. Adequately trained health-care workers are needed to bolster the drug’s efficacy and safety, especially during potentially intense, unpredictable and lengthy psychedelic experiences.

Existing treatments for mental-health conditions, including psychotherapy and antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, can be extremely effective for some people. But their full therapeutic benefits can take time to emerge. The rapid relief provided by psychedelics could complement such therapies.

However, even the most sophisticated and effective treatment strategies will have limited impact if people can’t access them. That’s why funders and regulators must work out who is going to cover the cost of a brain scan (if they are found to be clinically useful) or pay for a hours-long session so people can take psychedelics safely. Someone will need to assess whether these approaches have enough benefits to offset the spiralling costs of mental-health care — and whether those benefits can be provided equitably.

US speeds up research into mind-altering drugs — including mysterious ‘ibogaine’

There are ways to reduce upfront costs as well as expand reach, for example, by using low-cost biomarkers and therapy sessions in which participants take psychedelic substances together in a supervised setting. Several studies have found that such group sessions can even enhance the therapeutic effects in some cases (A. L. Back et al. Psychedelic Med. 4, 209–221; 2026). Psychedelics with briefer hallucinogenic effects, currently under development, might be an alternative, too.

However, progress on diagnoses and treatments should be paired with innovation on another front: preventing people from developing a mental-health disorder in the first place. No medical breakthroughs can substitute for a society that supports good mental health — and more could be done to reduce the factors that contribute to mental illness, such as economic insecurity, sleep disruption, environmental pollution and social isolation.

The field’s willingness to consider how to reinvent psychiatry is welcome. Proponents of the ideas must now ensure that all who can benefit have access to these therapies and that the highest standards of quality and rigour are adhered to.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on significant innovations in psychiatry, specifically the personalization of mental-health care and the development of psychedelic therapies, which have the potential to improve treatment outcomes for the over one billion people affected by mental health conditions globally. These advances address a major public health challenge with broad societal impact and include detailed context on methods, challenges, and the need for equitable access, fulfilling the criteria for inspiring good news.
articles.personality_title: New approaches in psychiatry bring hope through personalized care and psychedelics
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – More than one billion people worldwide live with mental health conditions, making these illnesses the leading cause of disability globally. Traditional treatments like antidepressants often don’t work for everyone, and mental health problems cost the global economy about $1 trillion each year.

**What happened** – Scientists and doctors are developing new ways to treat mental health problems by personalizing care and using psychedelic medicines. Personalization means matching treatments to each person’s unique symptoms and biology using tools like brain scans and data from smartphones. Psychedelic therapies use special drugs that can help the brain change its patterns, offering faster relief for some people who haven’t improved with usual treatments.

**Impact** – These new methods could make treatments more effective and faster for many people. Personalizing care recognizes that two people with the same diagnosis might need very different treatments. Psychedelics might help people who don’t respond to existing medicines. However, these treatments can be expensive and need trained professionals, so making sure everyone can access them is a big challenge.

**What's next step** – Researchers and health authorities need to continue testing these treatments carefully and figure out how to make them affordable and available to more people. They are also exploring ways to lower costs, like group therapy sessions with psychedelics. In the future, combining better treatments with efforts to prevent mental illness by improving social and environmental factors will be important.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Personalized psychiatry and new psychedelic therapies are promising steps toward more effective mental health care but must be developed carefully to reach everyone who needs them.

articles.personality_title_es: Nuevos enfoques en psiquiatría ofrecen esperanza con cuidados personalizados y psicodélicos
articles.personality_presentation_es:

Las terapias psicodélicas usan drogas especiales que pueden ayudar al cerebro a cambiar sus patrones, ofreciendo alivio más rápido para quienes no mejoran con los tratamientos habituales.

**Impacto** – Estos métodos podrían hacer que los tratamientos sean más efectivos y rápidos para muchas personas. Personalizar la atención reconoce que dos personas con el mismo diagnóstico pueden necesitar tratamientos diferentes. Los psicodélicos podrían ayudar a quienes no responden a los medicamentos actuales. Sin embargo, estos tratamientos pueden ser caros y necesitan profesionales capacitados, por lo que garantizar el acceso para todos es un gran reto.

**Próximo paso** – Investigadores y autoridades de salud deben seguir probando estos tratamientos con cuidado y encontrar formas de hacerlos accesibles y asequibles. También exploran maneras de reducir costos, como sesiones grupales con psicodélicos. En el futuro, combinar mejores tratamientos con esfuerzos para prevenir enfermedades mentales mejorando factores sociales y ambientales será clave.

**Frase clave** – La psiquiatría personalizada y las nuevas terapias psicodélicas son pasos prometedores hacia un cuidado de salud mental más efectivo, pero deben desarrollarse con cuidado para llegar a todos los que las necesitan.

articles.title: A single sauna session sends immune cells surging through your body
articles.summary: A new Finnish study reveals that just 30 minutes in a sauna can temporarily flood the bloodstream with additional white blood cells, potentially helping the immune system patrol the body and detect threats. The surprising response resembles the immune boost seen during exercise and may help explain some of the health benefits linked to sauna bathing.
articles.content:
A single sauna session may trigger a surprising response in the immune system. Researchers in Finland have discovered that spending just 30 minutes in a sauna, with a brief cold shower halfway through, causes white blood cells to surge into the bloodstream. These cells are essential to the body's defenses, helping identify and fight infections and other potential threats.

The findings suggest that sauna bathing may temporarily mobilize immune cells that normally remain in tissues, allowing them to circulate more widely throughout the body. This increased movement could help the immune system monitor for harmful pathogens, including bacteria and viruses.

During the study, researchers observed an increase in every type of circulating white blood cell they measured. Among them were neutrophils and lymphocytes, two important groups of immune cells. Neutrophils are often among the first defenders to respond to an infection, while lymphocytes include cells that recognize specific threats, produce antibodies, and help coordinate immune responses.

The increase was temporary. Within 30 minutes after the sauna session, neutrophil and lymphocyte counts had returned to their original levels.

How Sauna Bathing May Activate Immune Defenses

"This may indicate that sauna bathing mobilizes additional white blood cells into the bloodstream from tissues, where they are then redeposited after the session. This kind of periodic release of white blood cells into the bloodstream is beneficial, as once they leave their storage sites, they are better able to patrol the body and respond to pathogens," says Ilkka Heinonen, an Academy Research Fellow at the University of Turku.

This process is known as immune surveillance. Rather than remaining in one location, immune cells travel through the bloodstream and tissues, searching for signs of infection or other abnormalities. By temporarily increasing the number of white blood cells in circulation, the body may improve their ability to detect potential threats.

Interestingly, a similar response occurs during physical exercise. Exercise can temporarily increase the number of immune cells moving through the bloodstream, helping distribute them throughout the body. The new findings suggest that sauna bathing may produce a comparable short-term response, although this does not mean the two activities provide identical immune benefits.

Sauna Heat Also Affects Immune Signaling Molecules

The researchers also investigated whether sauna bathing influenced cytokines, small proteins that help immune cells communicate with one another. Cytokines play important roles in regulating inflammation, coordinating immune defenses, and directing the body's response to infections.

Overall, the sauna session produced little change in average cytokine levels in the bloodstream. However, a closer examination revealed an interesting connection between certain cytokines and changes in body temperature.

"Interestingly, however, the levels of several cytokines changed in relation to how much body temperature rose during sauna bathing. No similar association was observed between white blood cell counts and changes in body temperature," says Professor Jari Laukkanen, who led the study at the University of Eastern Finland.

In other words, some immune signaling molecules responded differently depending on how much a person's body temperature increased. White blood cell counts, however, did not show the same relationship with rising body temperature.

This distinction suggests that sauna bathing may influence different parts of the immune system through different physiological processes.

What This Discovery Means for Sauna Health Benefits

Previous research has linked regular sauna bathing with several potential health benefits. The latest findings offer another clue about what may be happening inside the body during these sessions, particularly how heat exposure and the sauna routine affect immune cell circulation.

However, the researchers caution that the results do not establish whether sauna bathing produces lasting improvements in immune function or reduces the risk of illness. The study examined only the immediate effects of one sauna session, and the observed changes in white blood cells were short-lived.

Because the session also included a brief cold shower, the findings reflect the combined sauna and cooling routine rather than the isolated effects of heat alone.

The research involved 51 adults with an average age of 50. The findings were published in the scientific journal Temperature, which specializes in research on body temperature regulation and its effects on human physiology.

Although more research is needed to understand the long-term implications, the study reveals that even a single sauna session can rapidly change how immune cells circulate through the body, potentially offering new insight into the biological effects of this popular relaxation practice.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a scientific study demonstrating that a single sauna session can temporarily increase white blood cell circulation, potentially boosting immune surveillance. This finding has broad health relevance for the general public, offering new insight into how sauna bathing may support immune function. The article provides detailed context about the study, its findings, and implications, making it a substantive and inspiring health-related discovery.
articles.personality_title: A single sauna session temporarily boosts immune cell circulation
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists in Finland studied how sauna bathing affects the immune system. Saunas are popular for relaxation and health, but this study focused on how just one session changes white blood cells, which help fight infections.

**What happened** – Researchers had 51 adults spend 30 minutes in a sauna with a short cold shower in the middle. They found that right after the session, the number of white blood cells in the bloodstream increased. These cells include neutrophils and lymphocytes, which protect the body by detecting and fighting germs. However, this increase was temporary and returned to normal within 30 minutes.

**Impact** – This study shows that sauna bathing can quickly send immune cells from tissues into the blood, allowing them to move around more and better watch for threats. This process, called immune surveillance, is similar to what happens during exercise. The findings help explain some health benefits people experience from saunas, especially how they might support the body's defense systems.

**What’s next step** – More research is needed to find out if sauna sessions have long-term effects on immune health or reduce sickness. Future studies might also separate the effects of heat from the cold shower and explore how different parts of the immune system respond to sauna heat.

articles.personality_title_fr: Une séance de sauna augmente temporairement la circulation des cellules immunitaires
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Des scientifiques finlandais ont étudié comment le sauna influence le système immunitaire. Le sauna est populaire pour la détente et la santé, mais cette étude s’est concentrée sur l’effet d’une seule séance sur les globules blancs, qui combattent les infections.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les chercheurs ont fait passer 30 minutes dans un sauna à 51 adultes, avec une courte douche froide au milieu. Ils ont constaté qu’immédiatement après, le nombre de globules blancs dans le sang avait augmenté. Ces cellules incluent les neutrophiles et les lymphocytes, qui protègent le corps en détectant et combattant les germes. Cette augmentation était temporaire et revenait à la normale en 30 minutes.

**Impact** – Cette étude montre que le sauna peut rapidement faire passer des cellules immunitaires des tissus vers le sang, ce qui leur permet de circuler davantage et de mieux surveiller les menaces. Ce processus, appelé surveillance immunitaire, est similaire à ce qui se passe pendant l’exercice. Ces résultats aident à comprendre certains bienfaits du sauna, notamment son soutien au système de défense du corps.

**Prochaines étapes** – Il faut encore des recherches pour savoir si les séances de sauna ont des effets durables sur la santé immunitaire ou réduisent les maladies. Les futures études pourraient aussi séparer les effets de la chaleur de ceux de la douche froide et examiner comment différentes parties du système immunitaire réagissent à la chaleur du sauna.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Passer seulement 30 minutes dans un sauna peut augmenter brièvement les cellules immunitaires dans le sang, aidant le corps à mieux repérer les infections.
articles.personality_title_es: Una sesión de sauna aumenta temporalmente la circulación de células inmunitarias
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Científicos en Finlandia estudiaron cómo el sauna afecta el sistema inmunológico. El sauna es popular para relajarse y la salud, pero este estudio se centró en cómo una sola sesión cambia los glóbulos blancos, que ayudan a combatir infecciones.

**Qué pasó** – Los investigadores hicieron que 51 adultos pasaran 30 minutos en un sauna con una breve ducha fría a la mitad. Descubrieron que justo después, la cantidad de glóbulos blancos en la sangre aumentó. Estas células incluyen neutrófilos y linfocitos, que protegen el cuerpo detectando y combatiendo gérmenes. Este aumento fue temporal y volvió a la normalidad en 30 minutos.

**Impacto** – Este estudio muestra que el sauna puede enviar rápidamente células inmunitarias de los tejidos a la sangre, permitiendo que circulen más y vigilen mejor las amenazas. Este proceso, llamado vigilancia inmunitaria, es similar a lo que sucede durante el ejercicio. Los hallazgos ayudan a explicar algunos beneficios para la salud relacionados con el sauna, especialmente cómo puede apoyar la defensa del cuerpo.

**Próximos pasos** – Se necesita más investigación para saber si las sesiones de sauna tienen efectos a largo plazo en la salud inmunológica o reducen enfermedades. Estudios futuros podrían separar los efectos del calor y la ducha fría y explorar cómo diferentes partes del sistema inmunológico responden al calor del sauna.

**Resumen en una frase** – Pasar solo 30 minutos en un sauna puede aumentar brevemente las células inmunitarias en la sangre, ayudando a que las defensas del cuerpo patrullen mejor para detectar infecciones.
